hello.note: Shared Islamic greeting, used same as in Urdu and Punjabi; reply: wa-uh-LAY-koom us-suh-LAAM.

good_morning.note: Native Saraiki-speaker sentence (Tatoeba), lit. 'dawn well'; distinct from the Urdu-style subh bakhair.

good_evening.note: Native Saraiki-speaker sentence (Tatoeba), same 'time-plural + khair' pattern as good_morning.

goodbye.note: 'God be your companion'; a farewell distinct from Urdu, confirmed in Saraiki Wiktionary and in wide use on Saraiki Wikipedia; khuda hafiz also used.

how_are_you.note: Confirmed as a native Saraiki-speaker translation on Tatoeba; a shorter variant, tusaan keenvin ho, is also attested there.

thank_you.note: Attested as a Saraiki headword on Saraiki Wiktionary and in wide native use on Saraiki Wikipedia; shared with Urdu/Persian.

youre_welcome.note: 'It is my pleasure'; khush (happy) is Saraiki-attested on Wiktionary, khushi is in wide native use on Saraiki Wikipedia, but the full phrase is an unconfirmed shared Urdu-register idiom. Rejected rivals: khush aamdeed is a false friend (means 'welcome' to an arriving guest, not a reply to thanks); koi gaal kaini would blur it with no_problem.

no_problem.note: 'No matter/thing'; kaini and gaal (with the Saraiki implosive ڳ) are both confirmed in native Saraiki-speaker sentences on Tatoeba and heavy Saraiki Wikipedia use. Corrects the plain-گ spelling, which on-wiki search shows is the personal name/flower 'Gul' instead.

please.note: 'By your kindness'; shared Perso-Urdu construction, but meharbani itself is in wide native use on Saraiki Wikipedia.

excuse_me.note: Literally 'listen', to get attention; shared across the region's languages.

sorry.note: Shared Arabic-root word for pardon/apology; in wide native use on Saraiki Wikipedia, though not a distinct Saraiki Wiktionary headword.

yes.note: Pan-regional yes, in heavy native use on Saraiki Wikipedia, but the Saraiki Wiktionary entry for haan only lists 'am' and 'heart' senses, not 'yes', so this specific sense is not independently confirmed.

no.note: A hallmark Saraiki negator, distinct from Urdu/Punjabi 'nahi'; confirmed across many native Saraiki-speaker sentences on Tatoeba (e.g. Russian is not an easy language).

of_course.note: Rivals: bilkul (absolutely) has no Saraiki attestation found; theek (OK, confirmed on Tatoeba) answers a different question. Zaroor is a shared Perso-Arabic loanword used mainly as 'necessarily/definitely', but is the best-attested plain pick, in heavy native use on Saraiki Wikipedia.

amazing.note: Common South Asian exclamation of admiration.

delicious.note: Shared with Urdu; mazedar itself is in native use on Saraiki Wikipedia, but a distinct Saraiki intensifier could not be confirmed.

cheers.note: The English word; toasting is not a local custom.
